::: {.why}
Daily equity returns have almost no linear predictability, and building the fitting machinery on a series where the answer is close to zero is the honest way to learn what a significant coefficient looks like.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Fit and interpret an ARMA model with statsmodels, including reading the coefficient standard errors correctly.
- State the magnitude of linear autocorrelation you actually find in daily equity returns, and say whether it is tradeable after a one basis point cost.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the autoregressive and moving average model sections of the ARIMA chapter of Forecasting: Principles and Practice, then fit ARMA(p,q) for p and q up to 2 on SPY daily returns using statsmodels. Report the coefficients with standard errors.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Turn the fitted coefficient into money: if the lag-1 coefficient is rho, the expected return conditional on yesterday is rho times yesterday's return. Compute the average absolute size of that conditional expectation in basis points, and compare it against a one basis point round-trip cost. This calculation is why nobody trades daily equity autocorrelation.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Repeat the fit on the monthly series and note that the sign flips. Write one line on what that could be other than a real effect.
:::
:::
